metadata.working_title: 22-year-old woman, fainted at home with a fever and a rash, walked in with her roommate
metadata.chief_complaint_patient_voice: I fainted in the shower. I've had a fever for two days and now I'm red all over.
metadata.final_diagnosis: Menstrual staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome from a tampon retained for about four days, with septic shock, acute kidney injury, thrombocytopenia, transaminitis and early rhabdomyolysis. Blood cultures are expected to stay negative, as they usually do in staphylococcal toxic shock.
learning_objectives: Recognize shock in a young, talking patient from the heart rate, the blood pressure, the capillary refill and the lactate, and do not let a plausible story of flu and a sunburn explain them away.
In fever, rash and hypotension with no clear source, ask about menstruation and tampon use and do a pelvic examination.
Remove the source. A retained tampon is found and removed at the bedside, and nothing else in the resuscitation replaces that.
Give about 30 mL/kg of crystalloid, reassess, and start norepinephrine when the mean arterial pressure stays under 65 after fluid.
Start antibiotics early that cover staphylococci including MRSA, and know why clindamycin is added in toxin-mediated disease.
Admit to intensive care, and name the organ injuries at handover.
metadata.teaching_frame: She looks well enough to send home, and the easy story is one every learner has heard a hundred times. The case is built so that the numbers contradict the patient's own explanation from the first second, and so that the one thing that changes her course is something nobody will mention unless the learner asks or looks.

patient.background:
Graduate student, lives with one roommate. No past medical history. Wisdom teeth removed at eighteen and no other surgery. Takes a combined oral contraceptive pill. She took ibuprofen yesterday, two tablets a couple of times, and nothing else. No allergies. Does not smoke, drinks socially, uses no drugs.

Her period started five days ago. She uses super-absorbency tampons. Four days ago she put one in before an evening out, came home late, and did not take it out. She believes her period has ended and has not thought about the tampon since. Two days ago she developed fever, chills, muscle aches and a sore throat, which she puts down to the flu. She has no vomiting and no diarrhea, and she has barely eaten or drunk since. Yesterday she took her temperature and it was 102. The same day she spent an hour at the beach and blames her red skin on that. This morning she fainted in the shower, for a few seconds by her roommate's account and without hitting her head, and her roommate drove her in. Rewritten on 11 October 2026 on author instruction: she presents fainting, febrile and with a rash, not with vomiting and diarrhea.
patient.presenting_vitals_source: Inherited from phase 'presentation'. Measured at triage.
patient.presenting_appearance: A young woman sitting up on the bed, talking in full sentences and apologizing for coming in. She is flushed red all over and her lips are dry. She does not look as sick as her numbers.
patient.ems_handover_text: Twenty-two year old woman, two days of fever, chills and body aches. She thinks it is the flu. Fainted in the shower this morning, out for a few seconds by her roommate's account, no head strike. Heart rate 128 and pressure 94 over 58 at triage, temperature 39.4. She looks sunburned and says she was at the beach yesterday. Walking, talking, roommate with her.
patient.arrival_handover: Twenty-two year old, fever for two days and red all over since yesterday. She fainted in the shower this morning and her roommate drove her in.
patient.handover_authoring_note: Section 2.3. Two sentences, 26 words, in a triage nurse's voice. No vital sign, no past history, no medication, no pertinent negative, and no diagnosis in clinical or lay words. Rewritten on 11 October 2026: the presentation is fainting, fever and a rash. The period is left for the learner to find. The earlier wording repeated her 'something she ate', a recorded exception to section 11.5 that no longer applies.

phase_notes.count_justification: Six clinical phases, the ceiling the authoring document set at the time, and one terminal. They are the natural history (compensated, transient response to fluid, hypotensive) crossed with what the learner has done about it (a vasopressor with the source in, the source out) plus one deterioration for a learner who does neither.
phase_notes.no_halted_phase: Nothing in this case is tagged harmful and there is no halted phase and no arrest. Every wrong turn is recoverable. That follows the design guide ('failure is safe, visible and owned') and AFRVR's v0.20 precedent.
phase_notes.the_intended_path_goes_through_hypotensi: On the directing physician's decision the learner is expected to see the fluid response fade and then start norepinephrine. The hypotensive phase is a waypoint, not a failure.
phase_notes.antibiotics_move_nothing: No antibiotic changes a phase or a vital sign. That is deliberate: their benefit is not visible in an emergency department stay, and showing one would be false. They are scored and prompted, and the debrief says why the monitor did not move.

phases.label: Compensated shock, looks well
phases.clinical_description: Alert, talking, flushed and febrile. Tachycardic with a low-normal pressure and a narrow margin. Capillary refill is slow and the lactate is raised. She has had nothing but sips for two days and has a retained tampon nobody knows about.

ecg.author_note: Sinus tachycardia with narrow complexes in every phase, with the PR, QRS and QTc the ECG report gives. Model output.

transitions.author_note: First in every list so that a handoff is never overtaken by a clinical rule in the same step.

transitions.narration: She stood up to get dressed and went straight down. I've got her back on the bed. She's gray and drowsy and her pressure has dropped.
transitions.debrief_note:
She was discharged with a heart rate over 110 and a fever, and she fainted when she stood up. She is both dry and vasodilated. A young adult in that state holds a blood pressure with her heart rate, and standing takes that away.

The trap was the story. The flu and a day at the beach seem to explain the fever and the red skin, and fluid makes most people feel better. They do not explain a fit 22 year old who fainted, with a low pressure and slow capillary refill. A patient you are about to send home should have vital signs you would accept at home.
transitions.author_rationale: A delayed consequence of the learner's own action, so the five-second floor applies. Orthostatic syncope in compensated distributive shock is plausible. That it happens every time is a teaching choice. Model output, needs a physician's signature.

transitions.narration: That fluid is in. Her pressure is better and she says she feels a bit better.
transitions.debrief_note:
The first bolus helped, as it should. She was dry from two days of fever and barely drinking, and she is leaking fluid out of her vessels.

Read the response as information, not as a result. A patient who is still tachycardic with a temperature over 39 after a liter was not only dehydrated. The target is about 30 mL/kg, which for her is close to two liters, followed by a reassessment.
transitions.author_rationale: A delayed consequence of the learner's own action. Ten seconds stands for the time a liter takes to run in, heavily compressed. The size of the response is a teaching choice. Model output.

transitions.narration: She's gone gray and she's getting drowsy. Her pressure has dropped and her rate is up.
transitions.debrief_note:
She was given no fluid bolus and she stopped compensating. On arrival she was already in shock: a heart rate of 128, a pressure of 94 over 58, a slow capillary refill and a fever. She was holding her pressure with her heart rate.

Young patients do this well and then fail quickly. The time to treat shock is while the patient is still talking to you.
transitions.author_rationale: Deterioration on inaction. Untreated toxic shock progresses to hypotension over hours, and five minutes of case clock stands for that. The number is a drafting judgment and needs a physician's signature. The nurse asks for a line at 45 seconds and for fluid at 60 and again at 170. In the default mode those are 135, 180 and 510, so the first fluid warning comes 120 seconds before this rule and the escalation is never heard.

phases.label: Transient response to fluid
phases.clinical_description: Better after the first bolus and still tachycardic and febrile. This is the phase in which she looks most like a patient who could go home. The response does not last.

transitions.when: flag pressor_running set AND flag source_removed set
transitions.narration: The fluid on its own isn't holding her any more, but the vasopressor is, and her pressure is steady.
transitions.debrief_note: The effect of the fluid faded, which is the natural course of this illness, and she did not drop because a vasopressor was already running and the source was out. Starting a vasopressor before the pressure falls is a reasonable choice in septic shock and the case accepts it.
transitions.author_rationale: The same clock as the unguarded rule below, so that the fade happens at one moment whatever was done. Listed first so a learner who has done everything goes straight to the stable phase. Model output.

transitions.narration: The fluid on its own isn't holding her any more. The vasopressor is keeping her pressure up and I've had to turn it up.
transitions.debrief_note: The effect of the fluid faded and the vasopressor caught her. She is holding a borderline pressure on a rising dose, which means something is still driving the shock.

transitions.narration: That fluid isn't holding. Her pressure is back down, her rate is back up and she's getting drowsy.
transitions.debrief_note:
The response to fluid wore off. This is expected in toxic shock and is not a mistake on your part. The toxin dilates vessels and makes them leak, so crystalloid leaves the circulation soon after it goes in.

This is the moment the case is built around. A mean arterial pressure under 65 that persists after fluid is an indication for norepinephrine. The usual fluid target is about 30 mL/kg, and a vasopressor does not have to wait for all of it. More fluid alone will buy less each time.
transitions.author_rationale: Scheduled natural history. The rules above it catch a learner who already started a vasopressor, so in effect this fires when none is running. Two and a half minutes stands for the hour or so over which a transient responder declares herself. Model output, needs a physician's signature. No prompt names a vasopressor in this phase, so this fade arrives unwarned in both modes. That is deliberate and follows the directing physician's fourth decision (TSS-SEED.md section 0 and section 4a).
transitions.unguarded_rationale: The fade is the illness and not a consequence of anything the learner did or did not do, and the physician directing this case asked for exactly this: the pressure stays under a mean of 65 after about 30 mL/kg and norepinephrine is then the expected move. The nurse says after the first bolus that 30 per kilo is nearly two liters, and the phase this leads to is recoverable with one order.

phases.label: Hypotensive shock
phases.clinical_description: Mean arterial pressure 54. Drowsy but rousable, gray, tachypneic. Reached when the fluid response fades, when no fluid was given, or when she was stood up to go home. Fluid and a vasopressor together get her out.

transitions.narration: The vasopressor is working. Her pressure is up and she's more awake.
transitions.debrief_note: The vasopressor restored her pressure, and it is holding because the source is out. Ten seconds is a compression of the several minutes a titration takes.

transitions.when: flag pressor_running set AND flag fluids_given set
transitions.narration: The vasopressor has brought her pressure up and she's more awake. I've had to go up on it twice to get there.
transitions.debrief_note: The vasopressor restored a borderline pressure. She needs a rising dose to stay there, which is what an untreated source looks like from the infusion pump.

transitions.when: NOT flag pressor_running set OR NOT flag fluids_given set
transitions.narration: I can barely rouse her. Her pressure has dropped again and her rate is higher.
transitions.debrief_note:
Her mean arterial pressure stayed under 65 without both fluid and a vasopressor, and she progressed to profound shock.

Hypotension that persists after fluid is not treated with more waiting or with fluid alone. Norepinephrine can be started through a good peripheral line while central access is arranged. A vasopressor without any fluid is also not enough in a patient this dry.
transitions.author_rationale: Deterioration on inaction. The nurse asks for norepinephrine at 30 seconds and again at 120, and for fluid at 60 if none has been given. In the default mode those are 90, 360 and 180, so both first warnings come at least 60 seconds before this rule and the escalation is never heard. Four minutes is a drafting judgment and needs a physician's signature.

phases.label: On a vasopressor, source still in place
phases.clinical_description: Awake again with a mean arterial pressure of 64 on a vasopressor, and the dose is climbing. Fluid and a vasopressor are treating the consequence. The tampon is still there and the toxin is still being made.

transitions.author_note: First in every list so that a handoff is never overtaken by a clinical rule in the same step.

transitions.narration: I've stopped having to go up on the vasopressor since that came out. She's holding her pressure on the same dose.
transitions.debrief_note:
Removing the tampon stopped the decline. It did not cure her: the toxin already absorbed keeps acting for many hours, and she stays on a vasopressor. What changed is that the dose stopped rising.

The case shows this within seconds. In a real patient you would see it over the next hour or more, and you would not be able to tell it apart from the effect of everything else you did. That is the reason source control is done on principle and not judged by the monitor.
transitions.author_rationale: A delayed consequence of the learner's own action. The physician directing this case chose 'stops the decline, no dramatic rebound'. Ten seconds is a heavy compression and the debrief note says so. The speed of real improvement after tampon removal is unsourced. Needs a physician's signature.

transitions.narration: I've been going up and up on the vasopressor and it isn't enough any more. Her pressure has dropped, her rate is up, and I can barely rouse her.
transitions.debrief_note:
She had fluid and a vasopressor and still got worse, because the source was never removed. A retained tampon colonized with toxin-producing staphylococci keeps delivering toxin for as long as it stays in.

Shock that needs a rising vasopressor dose after adequate fluid means the cause is still active. Go back and look for it: a full examination including the pelvis, wounds, lines and packing.
transitions.author_rationale: Deterioration on inaction. The nurse asks whether anyone has examined her fully at 60 seconds and asks about her period at 180. In the default mode those are 180 and 540, so the first warning comes 90 seconds before this rule and the escalation is never heard. Four and a half minutes is longer than the other clocks on purpose: the directing physician asked that treated sepsis with a missed source decline more slowly. Needs a physician's signature.

phases.clinical_description: Mean arterial pressure 43, obtunded, mottled. Reached from the hypotensive phase without fluid and a vasopressor, or from the supported phase with the source still in. Not terminal. Fluid, a vasopressor and source removal together get her out.

transitions.narration: She's coming back. Her pressure is up on the vasopressor, her rate is down, and she's opening her eyes to my voice.
transitions.debrief_note: She recovered a pressure once all three things were done: fluid, a vasopressor and removal of the source. She spent time at a mean pressure in the 40s on the way, and her kidneys and liver will show it over the next days.
transitions.author_rationale: A delayed consequence of the learner's own action. That recovery from this phase is always possible is a teaching choice: the case has no death, so a learner who gets here can still find the answer. Model output.

flag_namespace_note: Flags are permanent. fluids_given is set by any crystalloid bolus and fluids_30mlkg by the second one. pressor_running is set by norepinephrine, the three infusions it covers, and dopamine. case_actions.debrief_note: The monitor is dark until it is attached. In this case the numbers are the whole argument against the story she tells: a heart rate of 128, a pressure of 94 over 58 and a temperature of 39.4 in someone who says she has the flu.

case_actions.debrief_note: Everything she needs goes through a vein: fluid, antibiotics and a vasopressor. A large peripheral line is enough to start all three, including norepinephrine.
A second line lets fluid run beside a vasopressor and antibiotics. Worth having in any patient in shock.

prompt.text: Her heart rate is fast, her pressure is soft, and she's kept nothing down for two days. Do you want a fluid bolus?

escalation.text: She still hasn't had a fluid bolus. She is dry and she needs volume. Can I hang a liter?

case_actions.debrief_note:
Crystalloid is the first treatment for septic shock, and the usual target is about 30 mL/kg in the first hours. She weighs 62 kg, so that is close to two liters. Guidelines suggest a balanced crystalloid over saline. Both are accepted here.

Two things to take from how she responded. The first liter helped and the help did not last, because toxic shock dilates vessels and makes them leak. And once her mean pressure was under 65 after fluid, more fluid alone moved the number for a minute and no longer. That pattern is the indication for a vasopressor.

The 30 mL/kg figure is a guideline default with weak evidence behind the exact number. It is a starting point for reassessment, not a dose to complete before thinking. [UNVERIFIED, confirm against the current Surviving Sepsis guideline]

case_actions.nurse_alert: That's running at a maintenance rate. It isn't a bolus.
case_actions.debrief_note: A maintenance infusion is not a bolus. Crystalloid is the first treatment for septic shock, and the usual target is about 30 mL/kg in the first hours, which for her is close to two liters. An infusion at a maintenance rate does not deliver that. The case counts a bolus as fluid resuscitation and does not count this.

escalation.text: She's a young woman with a fever, a rash and shock. Has anyone asked about her period? Do you want to examine her?

case_actions.debrief_note:
This is the action the case turns on. A tampon left in for four days was the site where Staphylococcus aureus was making toxin, and nothing given through a vein removes it.

Nobody will tell you it is there. She thinks her period is over and has forgotten the tampon. You find it by asking about menstruation and tampon use, or by doing a pelvic examination because a febrile patient in shock with a red rash has no other source. A CT of the abdomen and pelvis would also show it, later.

The idea that travels: septic shock without a source means you have not finished looking. Examine the places that are easy to skip, which are the pelvis, the perineum, the back, wounds, and anything packed or implanted.

In this simulator the pelvic examination has to come first, because you cannot remove what you have not found.

case_actions.debrief_note:
Norepinephrine is the first vasopressor in septic shock. The indication is a mean arterial pressure under 65 that persists after fluid. In this case that moment arrives when the effect of the first liters fades.

Starting it earlier, while a second liter runs, is also accepted here. Guidelines allow a vasopressor through a good peripheral line for a short time, so it should not wait for a central line.

Epinephrine, vasopressin and phenylephrine infusions count as the same act in this case. Norepinephrine is the one to reach for first. [UNVERIFIED, confirm against the current Surviving Sepsis guideline]

Dopamine raises the pressure and the case treats it as a running vasopressor. It is discouraged because it causes more arrhythmias than norepinephrine in shock, and she already has a heart rate over 120. Norepinephrine is first line. [UNVERIFIED: De Backer et al., NEJM 2010, the SOAP II trial]

prompt.text: She's febrile and in shock and nothing is covering MRSA yet. Do you want vancomycin up?

case_actions.debrief_note:
Antibiotics in septic shock are given as early as possible, after cultures if the cultures do not delay them. For suspected toxic shock the usual empiric regimen is vancomycin plus clindamycin. Vancomycin covers Staphylococcus aureus including MRSA until the swab and cultures say otherwise. Linezolid is an alternative some centers prefer, and it is not in this simulator.

Clindamycin is the other half. It stops bacterial protein synthesis and so reduces toxin production, which a cell-wall drug does not do. The support for this is laboratory and observational data, not trials. It is not scored in this case, and you should still give it.

The patient will not show you the benefit of either drug in the emergency department. Antibiotics change the next days, not the next minutes, and the case does not pretend otherwise. [UNVERIFIED, confirm regimen against current IDSA and local guidance]

The right drug to add. Clindamycin suppresses toxin production by stopping bacterial protein synthesis. It is given with vancomycin, not instead of it, because clindamycin resistance in Staphylococcus aureus is common enough to matter. Not scored in this case on the directing physician's decision. [UNVERIFIED: toxin suppression and the resistance rate]

Reasonable broad cover while the source is unknown. Fever, rash and shock in a young adult also raise meningococcal disease, which ceftriaxone treats. A broad beta-lactam does not replace vancomycin and clindamycin here, and adding one is not penalized.

Covers methicillin-susceptible staphylococci, which cause most menstrual toxic shock. It is a drug for after the susceptibilities are known. Empirically it leaves MRSA uncovered. [UNVERIFIED: that most menstrual toxic shock is methicillin-susceptible]

Sometimes given in severe toxic shock on the theory that it neutralizes toxin. The evidence is weak and is better for streptococcal than for staphylococcal disease. A decision for intensive care and infectious disease, and not scored here. [UNVERIFIED: the evidence for immunoglobulin]

Considered in septic shock that needs a rising vasopressor dose despite fluid. A reasonable later step and not a substitute for finding the source. [UNVERIFIED, confirm against the current Surviving Sepsis guideline]

Her kidneys are failing because they are not being perfused. A diuretic removes volume she does not have. The treatment for this kidney injury is restoring the circulation.

Fever and a rash make meningitis worth a thought. She has only a mild headache and no neck stiffness or photophobia, and she is in shock. Draw two sets before antibiotics when that does not delay them. In staphylococcal toxic shock the blood cultures are usually negative, because the illness is caused by toxin absorbed from a local site and not by bacteria in the blood. A negative culture does not argue against the diagnosis.
Her creatinine is 2.6 at age 22. Two days of flu does not do that without shock. This is one of the results that should end the flu story.

A high white count and a platelet count of 98. Thrombocytopenia with fever, rash and hypotension is multi-organ involvement and is one of the criteria used to define toxic shock syndrome. The hemoglobin is at the top of the range in a patient on day five of her period, which fits a dry patient.
A pregnancy test belongs in the workup of any woman of reproductive age with vomiting, fainting or abdominal symptoms. It is negative.

A metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation. Her fast breathing with clear lungs is that compensation.

Liver involvement: raised transaminases and bilirubin, and a low albumin. Kidney, liver, platelets and muscle are all involved in her, and that pattern is what separates toxic shock from flu or another viral illness.
Her creatine kinase is 2,140. That is muscle involvement, and it matches her muscle pain and tenderness. Muscle involvement is part of toxic shock, and with an injured kidney it needs watching.
Mildly prolonged clotting times with low platelets: early coagulopathy of sepsis.

A small collapsing vena cava and a vigorous ventricle: an empty, dilated circulation and a heart that is working.
A small volume of free fluid in the pelvis, which the CT of the abdomen also reports. No fluid anywhere else.
She needs intensive care: a vasopressor, organ support and close monitoring. Call early, with the lactate and the vasopressor dose.
Useful for the antibiotic plan and for the question of immunoglobulin.
Not needed to remove a tampon, which is a bedside procedure for the emergency physician. Reasonable afterwards for follow-up.

Her kidneys are failing because they are not being perfused, and the treatment for this kidney injury is restoring the circulation. Nephrology adds nothing tonight that the resuscitation does not. The kidney injury changes how every later drug is dosed, vancomycin first among them.

case_actions.debrief_note:
You chose to send her home while she still looked well, and she fainted on standing. The case let that play out instead of ending.

Before discharging anyone, read the vital signs as if you had not heard the story. A heart rate over 110 with a fever, a low pressure and a faint is not explained by the flu until everything else has been excluded.
Completion of the case. Scored on level of care and diagnoses.
Her airway is her own until she is obtunded.
A fast respiratory rate with clear lungs is compensation for a metabolic acidosis.
Capillary refill of four seconds with a thready pulse is shock, whatever the blood pressure reads. This examination takes ten seconds and contradicts the story.
Red eyes without discharge and a red tongue are mucous membrane signs of toxic shock. They are easy to miss if you are not looking for them.
A supple neck does not exclude meningitis. With no photophobia and a clear mind it makes it less likely.
A fast regular rhythm and a flow murmur. No sign of a failing heart.
Clear lungs. This is not a pneumonia, and she can take fluid.
A soft, non-tender abdomen. There is no abdominal source here, which is one more reason to keep looking.

The examination that finds the diagnosis. A pelvic examination is part of looking for a source in a febrile woman in shock, and it is the one most often left out. Do it with a chaperone and explain why.
No flank tenderness, which argues against a kidney source.
Diffuse muscle tenderness goes with the raised creatine kinase.

A diffuse red rash that blanches, like a sunburn, including places the sun does not reach. She has an explanation for it and the explanation is wrong. Petechiae that do not blanch would raise meningococcal disease, though early on the two rashes can look alike.
Alert and oriented early. Drowsiness later is cerebral hypoperfusion.
Calm and cooperative. Her wish to go home is not a sign that she is well.

prompt_cap_recommendation.rationale: Three. In the arrival phase a learner who does nothing hears the monitor at 20 seconds, the line at 45 and fluid at 60, and the fluid escalation at 170 is exempt from the cap. In the hypotensive phase the vasopressor prompt at 30 and the fluid prompt at 60 are the two the 240-second deterioration rests on, and with the line at 45 they are the first three. In the supported phase the source prompt at 60 is the one the 270-second deterioration rests on and it is the earliest. In the default mode every one of those is multiplied by three and still lands before its exit: 180 of 300, 90 and 180 of 240, 180 of 270. The vancomycin prompt at 110 is the fourth in the two shock phases on the do-nothing path and the cap silences it there.

authoring_notes.voice: A 22-year-old graduate student. Lay words, apologetic, minimizing. She is sure it is the flu and says so, which is her belief and not a diagnosis the case endorses.
authoring_notes.the_tampon: She does not volunteer it and it is a must-ask topic, so no other answer carries it. Asked about her period or tampons in any wording, she says she cannot remember taking the last one out. Section 8.4 holds: she reports what she knows and draws no conclusion from it.
authoring_notes.close_to_the_line: Two answers sit near the section 8.4 line and are flagged for the reviewer. The rash answer says the redness is under her shirt, and the genitourinary answer mentions a smell. Both are things a patient would notice and say. Neither names a cause.
authoring_notes.phrasings: The canonical question, hand-written variants and echo for forty topics are MGCA's, in case_4_variants.py. Three topics are this case's own: rash, suspect_meal and wounds_and_skin. EXTRA_VARIANTS adds eleven phrasings by hand, each under the topic whose answer covers it.
authoring_notes.changed_7_october_2026: After the audit a model edited these and no physician has read them. location_of_pain said her back was among the worst places and abdominal_pain said the pain was not in her back. The case's reasoning against a kidney source rests on no flank pain, so location_of_pain now says thighs and calves. The drowsy abdominal_pain answer gained 'Not my back.' Three topics gained facts (fever_and_chills, nausea_vomiting, current_medications), each restating part of its own answer. correct_disposition.label: Intensive care unit
correct_disposition.explanation:
She goes to intensive care. She is on a vasopressor, her lactate is raised, and her kidneys, liver, platelets and muscle are all injured. The toxin already absorbed keeps acting for many hours after the tampon is out, so she can keep getting worse over the next day.

What the receiving team needs to hear: the source and that it has been removed, how much fluid she has had, the vasopressor dose and whether it is still rising, which antibiotics went in and when, and the last lactate.

disposition_intercepts.when: (phase is presentation OR phase is fluid_responsive) AND NOT flag discharge_attempted set
disposition_intercepts.author_note: Decided by Aakash Setty on 6 October 2026: she faints and the case continues.

alternative_dispositions.label: Step-down or intermediate care with telemetry
alternative_dispositions.explanation: A step-down unit can watch her and cannot run this resuscitation. She needs a titrated vasopressor, an arterial line and one nurse who is not looking after three other patients. A patient on norepinephrine with four injured organ systems is an intensive care patient.

alternative_dispositions.label: General medical ward with telemetry
alternative_dispositions.explanation: Telemetry watches a rhythm. Her problem is her blood pressure and her organs, and the ward cannot titrate a vasopressor or repeat a lactate every hour.

alternative_dispositions.label: Emergency department observation unit
alternative_dispositions.explanation: Observation is for patients expected to go home within a day. A lactate of 4.6 and a creatinine of 2.6 took her out of that group before any treatment started.

alternative_dispositions.label: Discharge home
alternative_dispositions.explanation: She is in shock. The story of the flu and a sunburn fits her symptoms and does not fit her vital signs, her skin or her laboratory results. Sending her home is the error this case exists to prevent.

alternative_dispositions.label: Transfer to another hospital
alternative_dispositions.explanation: Everything she needs is in this hospital. In a hospital with no intensive care, transfer after the source is out and a vasopressor is running would be right.

correct_diagnosis.label: Toxic shock syndrome
correct_diagnosis.explanation:
Fever, a diffuse red rash that blanches, hypotension, and injury to several organ systems at once, in a menstruating woman with a retained tampon. That is menstrual staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome.

The diagnosis is clinical. It is made from the pattern and the source, and it does not wait for a culture. Blood cultures usually stay negative. The skin of her palms and soles is expected to peel one to two weeks from now, which confirms it too late to be useful.

Naming it matters at handover because it tells the next team three things: the source is out, clindamycin belongs in the regimen, and this can recur with tampon use.

additional_diagnoses.label: Septic shock
additional_diagnoses.explanation: She needed a vasopressor to hold a mean pressure of 65 after fluid, with a raised lactate. Saying so tells the receiving team how sick she is in the terms they use.

additional_diagnoses.label: Acute kidney injury
additional_diagnoses.explanation: A creatinine of 2.6 at age 22 with almost no urine. It changes how every later drug is dosed, vancomycin first among them. The ibuprofen she took at home may have added to it, and she should get no more.

additional_diagnoses.label: Lactic acidosis
additional_diagnoses.explanation: A lactate of 4.6 on arrival with a bicarbonate of 17. The repeat value is how the next team will judge whether the resuscitation is working.

additional_diagnoses.label: Rhabdomyolysis
additional_diagnoses.explanation: Her creatine kinase is 2,140 with muscle pain and tenderness. Muscle involvement is part of toxic shock, and with an injured kidney it needs watching.

additional_diagnoses.label: Retained vaginal foreign body
additional_diagnoses.explanation: The retained tampon found on the pelvic examination. It is the source, and the next team needs to hear whether it is out.

additional_diagnoses.label: Thrombocytopenia
additional_diagnoses.explanation: Her platelet count is 98, against a lower limit of 150. It is one of the organ systems involved.

additional_diagnoses.label: Anion gap metabolic acidosis
additional_diagnoses.explanation: Sodium 131, chloride 97 and bicarbonate 17 give an anion gap of 17, with a lactate of 4.6 on arrival.

additional_diagnoses.label: Hyponatremia
additional_diagnoses.explanation: Her sodium is 131, against a lower limit of 135.

additional_diagnoses.label: Hypokalemia
additional_diagnoses.explanation: Her potassium is 3.3, against a lower limit of 3.5.

alternative_diagnoses.label: Septic shock
alternative_diagnoses.explanation: True, and the resuscitation is the same. As the primary diagnosis it leaves out the cause. Septic shock is what is happening to her circulation. Toxic shock syndrome says why, and the why is what sends someone to look for a tampon and add clindamycin.

alternative_diagnoses.label: Sepsis
alternative_diagnoses.explanation: It understates her. She was hypotensive after fluid and needed a vasopressor, which is shock. It also names no source.

alternative_diagnoses.label: Viral gastroenteritis
alternative_diagnoses.explanation: She has no vomiting and no diarrhea, so this does not fit even her symptoms. It does not explain a temperature of 39.4 with a red rash, a creatinine of 2.6, platelets of 98 or a lactate of 4.6. When a common diagnosis does not explain the vital signs, keep looking.

alternative_diagnoses.label: Infectious gastroenteritis
alternative_diagnoses.explanation: She has no gut symptoms, and a gut infection does not cause a diffuse rash, liver injury and low platelets.

alternative_diagnoses.label: Hypovolemia
alternative_diagnoses.explanation: She is dry, and that is part of the picture. A patient who is only dry stays better after two liters. She did not.

alternative_diagnoses.label: Meningococcemia
alternative_diagnoses.explanation: The right thing to fear in a young adult with fever, a rash and shock, and covering it with ceftriaxone early is reasonable. The rash favors toxic shock. Hers is a diffuse redness that blanches, where meningococcal disease usually gives petechiae and purpura that do not. What settles it is that she has a source.

alternative_diagnoses.label: Urosepsis
alternative_diagnoses.explanation: Her urine has white cells in it, which is the trap. There are no bacteria and no nitrite, she has no flank tenderness and no burning. White cells without infection in the urine are a recognized finding in toxic shock.

alternative_diagnoses.label: Pyelonephritis
alternative_diagnoses.explanation: White cells in the urine without bacteria, nitrite, flank tenderness or urinary symptoms are not a kidney infection. They are part of toxic shock.

alternative_diagnoses.label: Scarlet fever
alternative_diagnoses.explanation: A red rash, a red tongue and a sore throat make this a fair thought. Scarlet fever does not cause shock with kidney, liver and platelet injury. When a streptococcal illness does, it is streptococcal toxic shock, which usually comes from a painful soft tissue infection that she does not have.

alternative_diagnoses.label: Heat stroke
alternative_diagnoses.explanation: She sat on a beach for an hour a day and a half after her fever started. The fever came first, her mind is clear, and heat stroke does not come with a retained tampon.

alternative_diagnoses.label: Heat exhaustion
alternative_diagnoses.explanation: The beach is her explanation for the rash, and it does not hold. She was febrile and aching a day and a half before she went.

alternative_diagnoses.label: Pelvic inflammatory disease
alternative_diagnoses.explanation: The pelvis is the right place to look and this is the wrong finding. She has no cervical motion tenderness and no pelvic pain. What the examination shows is a retained tampon.

alternative_diagnoses.label: Stevens-Johnson syndrome
alternative_diagnoses.explanation: Her skin is red and intact. There are no blisters, no target lesions and no mouth ulcers, and she has taken no new drug apart from ibuprofen yesterday.

alternative_diagnoses.label: Kawasaki disease
alternative_diagnoses.explanation: The red eyes, red tongue and rash overlap. Kawasaki disease is an illness of young children with five days of fever, and it does not present with shock and a retained tampon in an adult.

alternative_diagnoses.label: Rocky Mountain spotted fever
alternative_diagnoses.explanation: Fever, rash and low platelets fit. The rash of spotted fever is spotted and starts at the wrists and ankles. She recalls no tick exposure, which does not exclude it. The retained tampon is what makes toxic shock the better answer.

handoff.diagnosis_entry_method: The learner searches the whole diagnosis catalog and lists as many diagnoses as apply, the first being the primary.

clinical_domains.label: Recognizing shock in a patient who looks well
Things that look reasonable and are not

debrief_configuration.key_exams_note: Section 10.4. Every exam is tagged neutral, so the Physical score reads this list. These six are the ones that separate toxic shock from its mimics: perfusion, the rash, the pelvis, the mucous membranes, the neck and the abdomen. Model judgment, unreviewed.
debrief_configuration.intended_path_note: The intended path goes through the hypotensive phase. That is deliberate and it is the directing physician's decision: norepinephrine is the expected move once the mean pressure stays under 65 after about 30 mL/kg, so a learner who does everything right still watches the fluid response fade. A learner who starts a vasopressor during the fluid-responsive phase skips the hypotensive phase, which the case accepts.
debrief_configuration.trap_actions_note: Neutral actions that are worth a note when taken. The discouraged traps (discharge, rate control, ibuprofen, a diuretic, a lumbar puncture, early intubation) are surfaced by their tag and need no entry here.
cross_cutting_teaching_points: Read the vital signs as if you had not heard the story. A common diagnosis that explains the symptoms and not the heart rate, the fever or the skin is not yet the diagnosis.

Shock with no source means you have not finished looking. Ask about menstruation and tampons, and examine the pelvis, the skin, wounds and anything packed or implanted. Removing the source is treatment, and nothing given through a vein replaces it.

Clindamycin belongs beside vancomycin in suspected toxic shock. It reduces toxin production, which a cell-wall antibiotic does not. This case does not score it, and you will not see its effect in the department. The evidence is laboratory and observational.
A young patient holds a blood pressure until she cannot. Tachycardia, slow capillary refill and a raised lactate are shock, whatever the pressure reads.
A fluid response that fades is information. A mean pressure under 65 that persists after fluid is an indication for norepinephrine, and a good peripheral line is enough to start it.

Toxic shock syndrome is a clinical diagnosis: fever, a diffuse blanching red rash, hypotension, and three or more organ systems involved. Blood cultures are usually negative in the staphylococcal form.
White cells in the urine without bacteria are not a urinary infection. In this illness they are part of the syndrome, and treating them as the source ends the search early.
A fast heart rate that is holding up a blood pressure is not treated. Find the cause.
debrief_configuration.attempt_history_note: Blocked attempts are surfaced and not penalized. This case authors two. Removing a vaginal foreign body before the pelvic examination, where the nurse says nobody has looked yet. And stopping a vasopressor when none is running.
